notes.b: Read the labels and units before reading any value. Most lost marks come from a wrong unit, year or column.
points: Check the title, both axis labels, the key or legend, the units (%, thousands, millions, €m, hectares, mm, °C, per 1,000), the years shown and the source line.
Read a bar or line value by running a ruler from the top of the bar or point across to the vertical axis, estimating between gridlines, and quoting the value with its unit.
In a table, find the row and the column and read the cell where they meet; check the totals row before using a figure.
Compare two years by reading neighbouring columns; to spot the one that did not change, read across the whole row.
Highest and lowest: scan every value, not just the first and last. For a ranking, list the values from largest to smallest.
Count how many items are above an average line by counting the bars or points whose tops lie above it.
Twice as much: double the smaller value and look for the value that matches it.
Infographics combine headline numbers, icons, small charts and county maps on one page. Read each panel's own label and unit: headline figures are often totals, while panels may show percentages.

notes.b: A description states what the figure shows. An explanation states why it shows it.
points: Trend vocabulary: increase, rise or growth; decrease, fall or decline; steady, constant or no change; fluctuate; peak (highest point); trough (lowest point); gradual or rapid (sharp); levelling off.
The overall trend is the long-term direction. A short-term change, such as a single year's dip, is described separately.
To describe a trend, state the overall direction, the start and end values with their years and units, and the period of fastest change.
Name any peak, trough or reversal, and quantify the change as the difference, the percentage change, or both.
Point out anomalies: values that break the pattern of the others.
To compare two series, say which is higher, when the lines cross, whether the gap widens or narrows, and the difference in a given year (for example, net migration = immigration minus emigration).
To explain a trend, link the pattern to one cause from the relevant chapter, in one clause.

To evaluate a figure, check whether an axis that does not start at zero or has uneven intervals exaggerates change, whether unevenly spaced dates distort the trend, whether the sample is small, and whether the source is reliable and recent.
Percentages can hide small totals: a large percentage rise may be a small change in numbers.

notes.b: These worked values come from the invented (illustrative) population of six towns, in thousands: Town A 18, Town B 32, Town C 25, Town D 41, Town E 12, Town F 29.
points: Total (sum): 18 + 32 + 25 + 41 + 12 + 29 = 157 thousand (illustrative).
Difference: subtract the smaller value from the larger and say which is larger. Town B (32) exceeds Town C (25) by 7 thousand (illustrative).
Mean (average) = total of the values ÷ number of values: 157 ÷ 6 = 26.2 thousand, to one decimal place (illustrative).
Median: put the values in order (12, 18, 25, 29, 32, 41); with an even number of values, average the middle two: (25 + 29) ÷ 2 = 27 thousand (illustrative).
Mode: the most frequent value. The six towns have no mode because no value repeats.
Range = highest value minus lowest value: 41 − 12 = 29 thousand (illustrative).
Percentage of a total = part ÷ total × 100. Illustrative: Town D's share of the six towns is 41 ÷ 157 × 100 = 26.1%.
Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.
Always divide by the old (earlier) value. Illustrative Country P, broadband households: 20% in 2000 and 90% in 2025, so the percentage change is (90 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 350%.

Percentage points: when both values are already percentages, the change is a difference in percentage points. A rise from 20% to 30% is a 10 percentage-point increase, but a 50% increase in the percentage change, (30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100.

When a question asks by what percentage a percentage changed, the subtraction is the usual reading: give the answer in percentage points and add the percentage change if unsure. Use the percentage-change formula when the values are numbers rather than percentages.

Missing value X: parts of a whole add to 100% (pie chart or percentage table) or to a stated total (stacked bar or total row), so X = total minus the sum of the known parts. Illustrative Country Q: if all segments except 'other' total 85%, then other = 100 − 85 = 15%.
To find a number from a percentage: number = percentage ÷ 100 × total.
Rate per 1,000 = number ÷ population × 1,000. A birth rate is births ÷ population × 1,000.
Density = number ÷ area, given as people per km².
Ratio: compare two values as a ratio, e.g. 2 : 1. Illustrative: Town D (41) is more than three times the size of Town E (12), a ratio of about 3.4 : 1.
'Twice as much' means two times the other value; 'half' means divided by two.
Round to the precision the data uses, or to one decimal place where needed, and keep the unit and the multiplier (thousands, millions) in every answer.
In a calculation question, show the working: a correct answer with working is safe, and the working can earn marks if the answer slips.
Use graph paper, a sharp pencil and a ruler; draw the graph large enough to fill most of the space.
The title says what the data is, where and when, taken from the wording of the question.
The horizontal (x) axis shows categories or time; the vertical (y) axis shows values. Label both axes with units.
The scale starts at zero, is evenly divided, and its interval is chosen so the largest value fits (e.g. steps of 5 or 10 units).
On a line graph, time intervals are spaced in proportion to the years.
Plot every value accurately. Bars have equal widths and equal gaps; points are joined with ruled straight lines.
Use a key or legend whenever more than one colour or shading is used, and shade or colour each category distinctly.

notes.h: Worked example: drawing a bar chart (illustrative)
notes.b: Illustrative data: population of six towns, in thousands, from the totals block above.
points: Graph choice: a bar chart, because the values are one measure for separate towns.
Title: 'Population of six towns (thousands), illustrative'.
x-axis: 'Town', with Towns A to F in order.
y-axis: 'Population (thousands)', from 0 to 45 in steps of 5, so the largest value (41) fits.
Six bars of equal width with equal gaps, each drawn to its value: A 18, B 32, C 25, D 41, E 12, F 29.
A single data series needs no key; check each bar top against the scale before finishing.

notes.b: The question 'draw a suitable graph' is answered with one sentence of justification after naming the graph type. Each example below is illustrative.
points: Values for separate categories, e.g. the populations of six towns: bar chart.
Change over time, e.g. the percentage of an urban population from 1980 to 2020: line graph (a bar chart is usually also accepted).
Parts of a whole, or percentage shares adding to 100%, e.g. car sales by fuel type in one year: pie chart or divided bar.
Two related variables for the same places, e.g. income and birth rate for twenty countries: scatter graph.
Three components that add to 100%, e.g. sand, silt and clay at a soil site: triangular graph.
Age and sex structure of a population: population pyramid.
Monthly temperature and rainfall for one place: climate graph.
Values for areas on a map, e.g. population density by region: choropleth map.

notes.h: Bar charts, histograms and line graphs
points: Simple bar chart: separate categories, one bar per category, equal widths and equal gaps; vertical or horizontal.
Multiple (clustered or comparative) bar chart: two or more bars side by side per category, e.g. males and females, or two years; a key is needed.
Compound (stacked or divided) bar chart: each bar is split into components, and the top of the whole bar is the total.
To read a component in a compound bar, take the top of its segment minus the bottom of its segment.
Percentage compound bar: every bar reaches 100%, so the segments show shares rather than totals.
Illustrative Region R, tree planting: total 2,000 hectares, of which conifers 1,350 ha. Broadleaf = 2,000 − 1,350 = 650 ha, a share of 650 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 32.5%.
Histogram: like a bar chart but for continuous data grouped in classes (e.g. age groups or rainfall amounts), drawn with no gaps between bars.
Line graph (trend graph): one variable over time; plot the points at the correct years and join them with ruled lines.
Multiple line graph: two or more series on the same axes, with a key.
The gradient of a line shows the rate of change: a steeper section means faster change.

Illustrative Country P, households with broadband: 2000 20%, 2005 38%, 2010 61%, 2015 74%, 2020 86%, 2025 90%. The rise is continuous; the fastest change is 2005 to 2010 (+23 percentage points), and the rise slows to +4 points from 2020 to 2025 as the line levels off.
Illustrative Country P: the change from 2000 to 2025 is +70 percentage points, which is not the same as the 350% percentage change above.
Pie chart: parts of a whole. Degrees = percentage × 3.6, because 360° ÷ 100 = 3.6.
For raw numbers rather than percentages: degrees = value ÷ total × 360.
Drawing steps: draw a circle with a compass, draw a radius to 12 o'clock, then measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest segment first.
Shade, key or label each segment with its percentage, and check that the angles add to 360°.
Illustrative Country Q, electricity sources (gas 40%, wind 25%, solar 10%, coal 5%, hydro 5%, other 15%): angles 144°, 90°, 36°, 18°, 18° and 54°, totalling 360°.
Two pie charts compare the shares in two years, not the totals, unless the circles are drawn in proportion to the totals.
Divided (percentage) bar: a single bar split into shares that add to 100%, an alternative to a pie chart.

notes.h: Pictograms, population pyramids and the pyramid method
points: Pictogram: each icon stands for a fixed quantity stated in the key; a part-icon is a fraction of that quantity.
Population pyramid: a back-to-back horizontal bar chart, which is a histogram on its side.
Age groups, usually in 5-year bands, sit on the central vertical axis: 0 to 4 at the bottom and the oldest group at the top.
Males are drawn on the left and females on the right. The horizontal axis shows the percentage (or number) of the population, scaled outward from zero on both sides.

Reading a pyramid: a wide base means a high birth rate; a narrow top means low life expectancy; a narrowing base means a falling birth rate; bulges and indentations suggest baby booms, migration, war or famine.
Describe the dependent groups (young and old) and the working-age group when reading a pyramid.
The shapes of pyramids and the stages of demographic transition belong to the notes on Changing population characteristics.

Method for drawing one band (illustrative, Country Z): males aged 20 to 24 are 3.5% and females aged 20 to 24 are 3.4%. Draw a bar 3.5 units long to the left of the centre axis and a bar 3.4 units long to the right, at the 20 to 24 level.
Months J to D run along the bottom axis. Rainfall is shown as bars against a left-hand axis in mm.
Mean monthly temperature is shown as a line, plotted at the middle of each month, against a right-hand axis in °C.
From the graph, read the hottest and coldest months, the wettest and driest months, and the seasonal pattern (rain all year, or a wet and dry season).

Calculations from the graph: annual temperature range = maximum mean monthly temperature minus minimum; mean annual temperature = sum of the 12 monthly means ÷ 12; total annual rainfall = sum of the 12 bars.
Identifying a climate type from a climate graph is taught in the notes on Physical regions and the notes on Climatic environments and climate change.
Illustrative Station M, mean monthly temperature (°C) J to D: 5, 5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 16, 16, 14, 11, 8, 6. Rainfall (mm) J to D: 110, 80, 85, 60, 65, 70, 70, 85, 90, 115, 110, 120.
Illustrative Station M results: warmest in July and August (16°C); coldest in January and February (5°C); annual range 16 − 5 = 11°C; mean annual temperature 123 ÷ 12 = 10.3°C.

Illustrative Station M: total rainfall 1,060 mm; wettest month December (120 mm); driest month April (60 mm). Rain falls in every month with a winter maximum, and the mild winters and cool summers resemble a cool temperate oceanic pattern.
Scatter graph: two variables for the same set of places. The independent variable goes on the x-axis; each place is plotted as a point, and the points are not joined.
Draw a line of best fit by eye through the middle of the points.
Positive correlation: both variables rise together. Negative correlation: one rises as the other falls. No correlation: no clear pattern. Strength is described as strong or weak.
Outliers, or anomalies, are points that lie away from the pattern of the others.
Correlation does not prove cause.
Illustrative distance from a city centre and land value at eight sites: 1 km €900 per m²; 2 km €700; 3 km €620; 4 km €450; 5 km €400; 6 km €250; 7 km €260; 8 km €150.

Illustrative: the result is a strong negative correlation, with the 7 km site a slight anomaly because it is higher than the 6 km site. A one-clause explanation: accessibility falls with distance from the centre.
Triangular graph: shows three components that always total 100%, e.g. the percentage employed in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.
Each side is a 0 to 100% scale. Read each component along the gridlines parallel to the side where its 0 is, following the direction in which its numbers run.
Check that the three readings add to 100.
To plot a point: find the first value on its scale, follow its gridline in, and mark where it meets the second value's gridline; check the point with the third value.
A point clustered near a corner is dominated by the component that corner represents.

Illustrative employment structure: Country X is primary 10%, secondary 25%, tertiary 65%; it sits near the tertiary corner, typical of a developed economy. Country Y is primary 60%, secondary 15%, tertiary 25%; it sits near the primary corner, typical of a less developed economy.
Choropleth map: areas (counties, regions or countries) shaded by value class; darker shading means a higher value.
Classes must not overlap and must cover every value, e.g. 0 to 49, 50 to 99, 100 to 149, 150 and over. A key is essential.
Choropleth maps suit densities and percentages. Their weakness is that they imply the value is even across each area and hide variation inside it, and the boundaries look like sudden changes.

Illustrative regional population densities (people per km²): North 35, East 160, South 85, West 40, Midlands 60. North and West are the lightest shade and East the darkest; the empty 100 to 149 class still appears in the key.
Dot map: each dot stands for a fixed number, showing the distribution of a value.
Isoline map: lines join places of equal value, e.g. isobars, isotherms, isohyets or contours.
Flow-line map: arrow width is proportional to the amount moving, e.g. migration, traffic or trade.
Proportional symbols: circles or bars sized in proportion to the value, placed on the map.
Use a table rather than a graph when many exact values must be given. A table cannot show a trend at a glance.
Graphs, maps and tables are expected in the presentation of results in the Geographical Investigation report; the report's structure is in the notes on The Geographical Investigation (20%).

keyTerms.definition: The general direction in which a series of values moves over time, separate from short-term changes.
The highest point on a graph or the highest value in a data series.
The lowest point on a graph or the lowest value in a data series.
The arithmetic difference between two percentages, so 20% rising to 30% is a rise of 10 percentage points.
The average: the total of the values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when the values are arranged in order of size; the average of the middle two for an even number of values.
The value that occurs most often in a set of data.
The highest value minus the lowest value in a set of data.
A bar split into segments, where the height of the whole bar shows the total.
A bar chart for continuous data grouped into classes, drawn with no gaps between the bars.
A back-to-back bar chart showing the percentage of males on the left and females on the right in each age group.
A graph combining mean monthly temperature as a line (°C) and monthly rainfall as bars (mm) for twelve months.
A graph plotting two variables for the same places as unjoined points, used to show correlation.
The direction and strength of the relationship between two variables: positive, negative or none.
A straight line drawn by eye through the middle of the points on a scatter graph.
A value that breaks the pattern shown by the other values in a data set.
A graph showing three components that always total 100%, read on three scales.
A map of areas shaded by value class, where darker shading means a higher value.
A line on a map joining places of equal value.

factCards.term: Reading any figure: what to check before reading a value
factCards.definition: Read the title, both axis labels, the key or legend, the units (%, thousands, €m, mm, °C, per 1,000), the years shown and the source line. Most lost marks come from a misread unit, year or column.

factCards.term: Reading a value from a bar chart, line graph or table: the method
factCards.definition: Run a ruler from the top of the bar or point across to the vertical axis, estimate between gridlines and quote the value with its unit. In a table, find the row and column headings and read the cell where they meet; don't confuse a totals row or the wrong year's column with the value asked for.

factCards.term: Short data questions: how to find 'twice as much' and 'above the average line'
factCards.definition: Twice as much: double the smaller value and look for the value that matches it. Above the average line: count the bars or points whose tops lie above it. Highest or lowest: scan every value, not just the first and last.

factCards.term: Infographics and pictograms: how to read them without losing marks
factCards.definition: Read each panel's own label and unit: headline figures are often totals, while small charts and panels may show percentages. In a pictogram, check the key for what one icon stands for; a part-icon is a fraction of it.

factCards.term: Describing a trend in an answer: what to include
factCards.definition: State the overall direction; give the start and end values with years and units; name the period of fastest change and any peak, trough or reversal; quantify the change (difference and/or percentage change); point out anomalies.

factCards.term: Comparing two series on one graph: what to say
factCards.definition: Which series is higher; when the lines cross; whether the gap widens or narrows; the difference in a given year, for example net migration = immigration minus emigration.

factCards.term: Evaluating a figure (Higher): weaknesses to look for
factCards.definition: An axis that does not start at zero or has uneven intervals; dates far apart or unevenly spaced; a small sample; a source that is unreliable or out of date; percentages hiding small totals; treating correlation as proof of cause.

factCards.term: Percentage change: the formula and the common mistake
factCards.definition: Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100; a positive result is an increase and a negative result a decrease. Always divide by the old (earlier) value, never the new one.

factCards.term: Percentage points vs percentage change: how to answer when both values are percentages
factCards.definition: Subtract to give the change in percentage points, and add the percentage change if unsure. Illustrative: 20% rising to 90% is +70 percentage points but a 350% percentage change, (90 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100.

factCards.term: Percentage of a total, rate per 1,000 and density: the three formulas
factCards.definition: Percentage of a total = part ÷ total × 100; rate per 1,000 = number ÷ population × 1,000 (e.g. birth rate = births ÷ population × 1,000); density = number ÷ area, given as people per km².

factCards.term: Calculating a missing value X: the method
factCards.definition: Parts of a whole add to 100% (pie chart, percentage table) or to a stated total (stacked bar, total row), so X = total minus the sum of the known parts. To find a number from a percentage: number = percentage ÷ 100 × total.

factCards.term: Calculation questions: rules on rounding, units and working
factCards.definition: Round to the precision the data uses, or one decimal place; keep the unit and the multiplier (thousands, millions) in every answer; for a difference, say which is larger; show the working, which can earn marks if the answer slips.

factCards.term: Drawing a graph: rules for the paper, title and axes
factCards.definition: Use graph paper, a pencil and a ruler, and fill most of the space. The title says what the data is, where and when, in the question's wording. Categories or time go on the x-axis and values on the y-axis; label both with units.

factCards.term: Drawing a graph: rules for the scale, plotting and key
factCards.definition: The scale starts at zero, is evenly divided and fits the largest value (e.g. steps of 5 or 10). Plot every value accurately; bars of equal width with equal gaps; join points with ruled straight lines; a key if more than one shading is used.

factCards.term: Line graph: how to space the time axis
factCards.definition: Space the years in proportion to the time between them: for data for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2015, the last gap is half the others. Plot each point at its correct year and join the points with ruled lines; a steeper line means faster change.

factCards.term: 'Draw a suitable graph': which graph suits which data
factCards.definition: One value for separate categories: bar chart. Change over time: line graph. Shares of a whole adding to 100%: pie chart or divided bar. Two related variables for the same places: scatter graph. Three components adding to 100%: triangular graph.

factCards.term: Compound bar chart: how to read one component
factCards.definition: Take the top of its segment minus the bottom of its segment; the top of the whole bar is the total. In a percentage compound bar every bar reaches 100%, so the segments show shares rather than totals.

factCards.term: Pie chart: calculating the angles and drawing it
factCards.definition: Degrees = percentage × 3.6 (360° ÷ 100), or value ÷ total × 360 for raw numbers; angles must total 360°. Draw a circle with a compass and a radius to 12 o'clock, measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest first, and label each segment.

factCards.term: Population pyramid: how to draw the axes and bars
factCards.definition: Age groups in 5-year bands on the central vertical axis, 0–4 at the bottom and the oldest at the top; males on the left, females on the right; the horizontal axis shows % of the population (or number), scaled outward from zero on both sides.

factCards.term: Population pyramid: what four features of the shape tell you
factCards.definition: A wide base means a high birth rate; a narrow top means low life expectancy; a narrowing base means a falling birth rate; bulges and indentations suggest baby booms, migration, war or famine.

factCards.term: Climate graph: the calculations examiners ask for
factCards.definition: Annual temperature range = maximum minus minimum mean monthly temperature; mean annual temperature = sum of the 12 monthly means ÷ 12; total annual rainfall = sum of the 12 bars. Also read the wettest and driest months.

factCards.term: Scatter graph: drawing rules and how to describe it
factCards.definition: Put the independent variable on the x-axis; plot each place as a point and do not join the points; draw a line of best fit by eye. Describe the correlation (positive, negative or none; strong or weak) and any outliers. Correlation does not prove cause.

factCards.term: Triangular graph: how to read and plot a point
factCards.definition: Read each component along the gridlines parallel to the side where its 0 is, following the direction its numbers run. To plot: find the first value on its scale, follow its gridline in to where it meets the second value's gridline, and check with the third. The three always total 100%.

factCards.term: Choropleth map: rules for the classes and its weaknesses
factCards.definition: Classes must not overlap and must cover every value (e.g. 0–49, 50–99, 100–149, 150+); darker = higher; a key is essential. But it implies the value is even across each area, hides variation inside it and makes boundaries look like sudden changes.

questions.prompt: Examine the illustrative data showing the population of six towns, in thousands: Town A 18, Town B 32, Town C 25, Town D 41, Town E 12, Town F 29. Using graph paper, draw a suitable graph to illustrate this data.
questions.model: A bar chart is suitable because the values are one measure for six separate towns. Title: Population of six towns (thousands), illustrative. The x-axis is labelled Town, with Towns A to F in order. The y-axis is labelled Population (thousands) and runs from 0 to 45 in steps of 5, so the largest value (41) fits. Draw six bars of equal width with equal gaps, each drawn to its value: A 18, B 32, C 25, D 41, E 12, F 29. Marked elements: a clear title that says what, where and when; both axes labelled with units; an evenly divided scale starting at zero; accurate plotting of every value; equal bars with equal gaps.

questions.prompt: Illustrative data for Country P, percentage of households with broadband: 2000 20%, 2005 38%, 2010 61%, 2015 74%, 2020 86%, 2025 90%. (i) State the value in 2010. (ii) Name the five-year period with the fastest increase. (iii) Give the change from 2000 to 2025 in percentage points. (iv) Give the percentage change from 2000 to 2025, showing your working. (v) Describe the trend in three points, using figures.
questions.model: (i) 61% in 2010 (illustrative). (ii) 2005 to 2010, when the figure rose by 23 percentage points (61% minus 38%) (illustrative). (iii) 90 minus 20 = 70 percentage points (illustrative). (iv) Percentage change = (90 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 350% (illustrative). (v) The overall trend is a continuous rise, from 20% in 2000 to 90% in 2025. The fastest change was from 2005 to 2010. The rise slowed to 4 percentage points from 2020 to 2025, and the trend levelled off.

questions.prompt: Four illustrative calculations, each worth 2 marks, with working shown. (a) For a pie chart, what is the angle for a segment of 25%? (b) Six towns have populations, in thousands, of 18, 32, 25, 41, 12 and 29. What is their mean? (c) Mean monthly temperatures at Station M are 5, 5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 16, 16, 14, 11, 8 and 6 °C. What is the range? (d) Region R has a total of 2,000 hectares of tree planting, of which 1,350 hectares are conifers. What is the area of broadleaf?
questions.model: (a) 25 × 3.6 = 90 degrees (illustrative check: 25 percent of 360 is 90). (b) 18 + 32 + 25 + 41 + 12 + 29 = 157; 157 ÷ 6 = 26.2 thousand (illustrative). (c) Highest 16 °C minus lowest 5 °C = 11 °C (illustrative). (d) 2,000 − 1,350 = 650 hectares of broadleaf (illustrative).
